cls: Platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor inhibitor (monoclonal antibody Fab fragment)
pharm: The Fab fragment of the chimeric human-murine monoclonal antibody 7E3, given intravenously as an antiplatelet/antithrombotic adjunct during percutaneous coronary intervention; it binds the platelet glycoprotein (GP) IIb/IIIa receptor, blocking the final common pathway of platelet aggregation (fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor binding).

summary: Abciximab is the Fab fragment of a chimeric monoclonal antibody directed against the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor. Given intravenously as an adjunct to percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and, historically, in unstable angina when PCI is planned, it blocks the final common pathway of platelet aggregation by preventing fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor from binding the GP IIb/IIIa receptor, thereby reducing acute ischemic cardiac complications. It is used with aspirin and heparin. The principal risks are bleeding (including major and intracranial hemorrhage) and acute, sometimes profound, thrombocytopenia, which requires platelet monitoring before, during, and after dosing. Readministration carries an added risk of hypersensitivity and thrombocytopenia due to human anti-chimeric antibodies.
indications: Adjunct to percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to prevent acute cardiac ischemic complications in patients undergoing PCI
Patients with unstable angina not responding to conventional therapy when PCI is planned within 24 hours (historical labeled use)

dosage.d: 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus given 10-60 minutes before the procedure, followed by a continuous infusion of 0.125 mcg/kg/min (maximum 10 mcg/min)
dosage.n: Use with aspirin and weight-adjusted heparin; maximum infusion rate 10 mcg/min

dosage.c: Unstable angina with planned PCI within 24 h
dosage.d: 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus, then 10 mcg/min infusion for 18-24 hours, concluding ~1 hour after the PCI
dosage.t: Bolus then up to 18-24 hour infusion
dosage.n: Historical regimen; concurrent aspirin and heparin

admin: Administer intravenously; filter the bolus and the infusion through a sterile, non-pyrogenic, low-protein-binding 0.2/0.22 micron filter
Give through a dedicated/separate IV line where possible; do not add other medications to the infusion
Establish vascular access carefully and minimize arterial/venous punctures, IM injections, urinary catheters, and nasotracheal procedures to reduce bleeding
Use with aspirin and weight-adjusted heparin; titrate/avoid heparin per ACT to limit bleeding
Obtain baseline platelet count, hemoglobin/hematocrit, and coagulation studies, and recheck platelets 2-4 hours after the bolus and at 24 hours
moa: Abciximab is the Fab fragment of the chimeric human-murine monoclonal antibody 7E3. It binds to the glycoprotein (GP) IIb/IIIa (alpha-IIb/beta-3 integrin) receptor on the surface of activated platelets, which is the final common pathway for platelet aggregation. By occupying this receptor, abciximab prevents the binding of fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, and other adhesive ligands that cross-link platelets, thereby inhibiting platelet aggregation regardless of the activating stimulus. It also binds the vitronectin (alpha-v/beta-3) receptor on platelets and vessel-wall cells. Receptor blockade is dose-dependent; platelet function recovers gradually over 24-48 hours after stopping the infusion as the drug redistributes, even though free plasma levels fall quickly.

absolute: Recent (within 6 weeks) clinically significant GI or GU bleeding
History of cerebrovascular accident within 2 years or with significant residual deficit
Recent major surgery or trauma (within ~6 weeks), intracranial neoplasm, arteriovenous malformation, or aneurysm
Use of oral anticoagulants within 7 days unless INR is acceptable
Known hypersensitivity to abciximab or to murine proteins
relative: Advanced age and low body weight
Prior exposure to abciximab (risk of hypersensitivity and thrombocytopenia)
monitor: Platelet count (baseline, 2-4 hours after bolus, and at 24 hours)
Hemoglobin/hematocrit and clinical signs of bleeding
Activated clotting time (ACT)/aPTT to guide heparin
Signs of hypersensitivity, especially on readministration

preg: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Abciximab should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit clearly justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: It is not known whether abciximab is excreted in human milk. Because many proteins are excreted in milk and given the potential for adverse effects, caution should be used; consider not breastfeeding during and shortly after therapy.
renal: No formal renal dosing adjustment is provided, but patients with renal impairment (including those on dialysis) have an increased risk of bleeding. Use with caution, weigh the bleeding risk carefully, and monitor closely.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is described. Assess overall bleeding risk; abciximab is a protein cleared by proteolysis rather than hepatic metabolism.

major: Other antithrombotic/antiplatelet agents and thrombolytics (heparin, warfarin, NSAIDs, dipyridamole, ticlopidine, fibrinolytics) - markedly increased bleeding risk (heparin and aspirin are used together with it per protocol with monitoring)
moderate: Dextran and other agents affecting platelets/coagulation - additive bleeding risk
interactions.alcohol: Not relevant in the acute procedural setting.
interactions.diagnostics: Causes prolongation of bleeding time and inhibition of ex vivo platelet aggregation; monitor platelet count, hemoglobin/hematocrit, and ACT/aPTT for heparin dosing.

serious: Major hemorrhage including gastrointestinal and retroperitoneal bleeding
rare: Human anti-chimeric antibody formation with reactions on readministration

monitoring: Platelet count at baseline, 2-4 hours after the bolus, and at 24 hours (watch for acute thrombocytopenia)
Hemoglobin/hematocrit and clinical signs of bleeding
Vascular access/sheath site for hematoma or bleeding
Activated clotting time and aPTT to guide heparin
Vital signs and signs of hypersensitivity, particularly with repeat exposure
counsel: This medicine is given through a vein during your heart procedure to help keep blood from clotting on the stent
It can cause bleeding - tell the team about any bleeding, bruising, blood in urine or stool, severe headache, or weakness
You will have blood tests to check your platelets and blood counts before, during, and after treatment
Stay still and follow instructions about the catheter site to prevent bleeding
Tell staff right away about any rash, swelling, itching, or trouble breathing
Let your team know if you have ever received this drug before, as reactions can occur on repeat use
pk: Rapid platelet inhibition within minutes of the IV bolus
Maximal GP IIb/IIIa receptor blockade shortly after bolus
Initial ~10 minutes (free drug); platelet-bound function recovers over 24-48 hours
Platelet aggregation gradually returns toward normal over 24-48 hours after stopping
Refrigerate at 2-8 C; do not freeze or shake; do not use if particulates are present
pearls: Fab fragment of monoclonal antibody 7E3 - blocks the final common pathway (GP IIb/IIIa) of platelet aggregation during PCI
Two key risks are bleeding and acute, sometimes severe, thrombocytopenia - check platelets 2-4 hours after the bolus and at 24 hours
If life-threatening bleeding or severe thrombocytopenia occurs, stop the infusion; platelet transfusion can be used to reverse the antiplatelet effect
Used together with aspirin and weight-adjusted heparin; minimize vascular punctures and invasive procedures to limit bleeding
Readministration risks hypersensitivity and thrombocytopenia from human anti-chimeric antibodies
Biologic - often absent from openFDA structured data; dosing and warnings follow the FDA package insert (ReoPro) / EMA SmPC
missed: Abciximab is administered as a one-time bolus and short infusion by clinicians during a hospital procedure; there is no patient self-administered or missed-dose scenario. Dosing/timing is managed entirely by the treating team.
overdose: There has been no experience of acute overdose in humans; the main concerns are bleeding and thrombocytopenia. If overdose or serious bleeding occurs, stop the infusion immediately. Because abciximab binds platelets, platelet transfusion may restore platelet function and is used to manage major bleeding or profound thrombocytopenia, along with general supportive measures.
